## Phase I — The advisory war and escalation (Jan 1964 – Jul 1965)

### How the phase ends (changed)

By the end of July 1965 the advisory war is over. The decision to commit US ground forces in strength has been taken, the 173rd Airborne Brigade and the III Marine Amphibious Force are in the country, the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) is preparing to sail, and Rolling Thunder is in its fifth month. On the other side, the Viet Cong have formed regiments and divisions in the provinces around Saigon and in the coastal lowlands, PAVN regular regiments are in the Central Highlands, and the summer offensive has broken ARVN battalions at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai faster than they could be rebuilt, though none of the general reserve has been wiped out. In the countryside, the Viet Cong infrastructure administers, taxes and conscripts in a large share of the hamlets, and outside the held belt the government's pacification effort has nothing like the stable administration or the local security it needs. Inside it the summer is not the historical one: about 330,000 hectares of rice land have been titled to about 270,000 families, rent is no longer paid in most of the districts the government holds, and in those districts the government's arrival no longer means the landlord's¹. Where the government does not hold the hamlets at night, nothing has changed except the promise.

In Saigon, the Thieu–Ky junta has just taken power after a year and a half of coups. In Washington, the war has an open-ended authority from Congress and a decision on troops announced without the reserves, without a tax increase and without a declaration. In Hanoi, the Politburo has committed itself to winning before the Americans arrive in strength and must now decide whether to fight them. It will: in October the PAVN regiments of the B3 Front will go after the camp at Plei Me, and the Ia Drang will follow. The war that Phase II inherits is a war between two armies that each believe they can outlast the other, fought over a population that neither government has secured.

About 1,100 village posts are settled, two-thirds of the chiefs have come from the list, and the infrastructure has begun to leave the villages around the posts². The sea route to the coast is closed and the Cambodian route open, and the enemy's rear is on the U-2S's maps while his regiments under the canopy and his cadres in the hamlets are as hidden as before. The general reserve enters Phase II weakened but whole, and the Front enters it with between 10,000 and 30,000 of the Republic's carbines³. On Guam the B-52Js hold about 1,400 measured targets in the cell's folders and authority to strike none of them in the North.

Phung Hoang ends the phase with about 140 district centres open, every one behind a settled post, and a method that has reached above the hamlet in one district on the edge of Saigon and in a dozen in the Delta⁴. About 1,100 selected advisers are in the subsectors and battalions, speaking to their counterparts without interpreters; the rest of the field posts are still held on the old tour. The Front has begun to move its district committees out of the held belt, which costs it the villages' daily obedience and gains it the safety of the contested edge.

By the end of July 1965 the board has filled about 70 of the army's roughly 190 manoeuvre battalion commands and relieved its first nine commanders; the rest are still held by men the generals put there, and about a third of all battalions are still commanded by captains, because the army is short of majors and the career-course gate makes none faster⁵. The companies are led almost everywhere by the classes of 1957–63. The generals are the generals of 1963, and every one of them has learned that the board can be bargained with and cannot be ignored.

The Directorate ends the phase with its plants at about half their capacity and the domestic share four months old; about 5,000 PF radios, 6,000 hamlet radios and 600,000 dry cells have gone to the held belt, and the Front's mines in Long An have Go Vap batteries in them⁶. Route 1 on the coast has been reopened after the worst flood in memory, and the Front has an industrial working class in Bien Hoa to organise.

The army that enters Phase II has trained every private it has enlisted for eight years, and every territorial; it has kept about 2,000–3,000 of its best sergeants at the training centres to do it, in the two years it could least spare them, and the Muster Service has caught the centres that sold the course short. The general reserve was broken at Ba Gia and Dong Xoai and came back from both with more of its men than on any course before this one; the battalions are steadier than history's by a band, though the enemy still chooses where they fight⁷.

The NCO corps that enters Phase II has been schooled for its grades for eight years, regular and territorial alike, and about 1,300–2,500 of its best sergeants are teaching at Nha Trang, the division schools and the territorial centres, on top of the drill sergeants at Quang Trung⁸. The 4th Marine Battalion at Binh Gia and the 7th Airborne at Dong Xoai were broken and came back with more of their men than on either earlier course, because their sergeants took command when their officers fell. The enemy has the academy's leader's manual and has begun to teach its local forces the ARVN platoon's routine.

The combined command ends the phase as a channel, not yet a command. It survived Khanh's coup by passing every order through his office, and it learned in its first month that operational control means what the junta of the day allows. Seoul and Canberra have consented on conditions: a Korean countersignature on every order to a Korean formation, and an Australian casualty estimate sent to Canberra. The task force ends the phase about 1,100 strong, with one campaign that found nothing for two months and then broke the Can Giuoc security section from one notebook⁹. The Hoc Mon committee that STILL WATER drove out governs from Cu Chi, and the task force's III Corps task group has its name.

The North ends the phase without the fixed economy it began 1965 with. Its fuel is in drums, its power in village diesels, its bridges are pontoons by night, its fighters are in China, and four SA-2 battalions rotate among about twenty sites that the Js strike as they are built. About 300,000–400,000 of its people are already repairing and carrying full time, a year early, and the Politburo has held three divisions at home against a landing that is not coming¹⁰. The flow south is untouched, and the American decision of July is history's.

MACV-JSOC ends the phase four months old and Delta five, with 31 raids in the Saigon belt and the upper Delta, nine of them reaching a cadre the file had listed, and one operator dead at a doorway in Can Giuoc. Its one finished operation is NIGHT HERON, which took six of the eleven men of the Long An province committee at a sampan mooring with the province finance section's ledgers, and cut the Front's collections in three districts to about a third of the previous year's by December¹¹. The partnered cordon has been tried twice and abandoned, because a Ranger company told the hamlet what was coming and the battalion had to be told the night before. The unit has learned the country and has not yet learned what it will learn in Dinh Tuong: that the men it hunts can simply move, and that the price of its arrival is paid in the enemy's walking time.

### New: MACV-JSOC stands up and Delta arrives
*15 Aug – 31 Dec 1964 · Tan Son Nhut, Saigon; forward operating bases at Da Nang, Kontum, Bien Hoa and Can Tho · EV014-1*

*Initiative: allied*

COMUSMACV's order of 15 August 1964 created the Joint Special Operations Command, Vietnam, eleven days after the second report from the Gulf of Tonkin that this war never answered with Pierce Arrow. Brigadier General Harold M. Vance, lately of the Special Warfare Center at Fort Bragg, took it with a staff that reached 280 by December and 390 by the following June: a joint targeting cell, a joint operations centre that stood a watch from 18:00 to 06:00, and nineteen liaison cells — MACV J-2 and J-3, MACV-SOG, the CIA station, the Combined Interagency Task Force and its National Fusion Centre, the combined command's operations centre, the 2nd Air Division, the four US corps-level commands and the four ARVN corps headquarters, the Joint General Staff, the National Police, the US Mission and the Embassy in Vientiane¹¹. The headquarters held no authority anyone else had held: it could command the units assigned to it, declare a restricted operating area over a hamlet for a night, and claim a target from the task force's deck. It could compel nothing outside MACV.

The 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta came in three lifts of MATS C-135Bs and C-124s from Pope Air Force Base between 28 August and 12 September 1964, 1,310 officers and men under Colonel James E. Teague, with 288 operators in four assault squadrons and G Squadron; E Squadron's unmarked light helicopters came by sea to Saigon port on 24 September and flew from Tan Son Nhut from 2 October¹¹. Three squadrons went forward to Bien Hoa, Can Tho and Da Nang and one stayed at Tan Son Nhut to rest and retrain, which is the rotation the unit kept for the next eight years and the reason its sustained rate was never what its first month suggested.

The first three months were learning and they were cheap. Thirty-one raids were mounted in the Saigon belt and the upper Delta between 11 October and 31 December, all of them on addresses from the task force's Gia Dinh and Long An files; nine reached a cadre the file had listed at district level or above, and nineteen found the house empty or the wrong man in it. Teague's men did not know the country: the Delta's canal lines, the way a hamlet's dogs work, which path a cadre takes when he runs. On 14 and 22 November the squadron at Bien Hoa tried the concept it had brought with it, a Delta troop as the entry force with a company of the 32nd Ranger Battalion as the cordon, at Phu Hoa Dong and at Trung Lap. Both times the cordon moved into position before midnight and both times the house was empty by the time the troop reached it, and on the second the Rangers' battalion had been given the hamlet's name the previous afternoon. The concept was abandoned in December and nothing replaced it: from then on Delta went in without a cordon and accepted that some of the men in the house would get into the dark. The unit's first dead was Sergeant First Class Donald R. Keel, shot through the throat at a doorway in Can Giuoc on 2 December 1964; two more operators were wounded in the same ten weeks¹¹.

### New: Operation NIGHT HERON: the Long An province committee
*9 Feb – 18 Apr 1965 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be, Gia Dinh Province · EV014-2*

*Initiative: allied*

NIGHT HERON was the first operation that showed what the unit was for, and it was built on a file three other provisions had made. The task force's DRY SEASON campaign had broken the Can Giuoc security section from a notebook in December 1964; the section's papers named a courier, the courier's family was in the Special Branch's census, and the land register said whose house he slept in. What none of that could do was reach the eleven men of the Long An province committee, who met every third or fourth week at a sampan mooring on the Rach Cat where no police patrol had been since 1962.

Two men of G Squadron lay in the nipa palm 240 metres from the mooring for four nights between 9 and 23 February and for three more in March, counted the arrivals, and photographed six of them at ranges under 300 metres with a starlight-assisted camera. On the night of 14–15 March 1965 two assault teams and a Special Branch inspector came in by three of E Squadron's helicopters to a paddy 900 metres east, walked in on goggles, and took the mooring at 02:40. Six of the eleven committee members were there, with the province finance section's ledgers for 1964 and a list of the collectors in nineteen villages; two cadre who reached for weapons were killed, the committee's secretary got into the Rung Sat with the political officer, and one Delta operator was shot through the forearm. The task force's exploitation cell at Tan Son Nhut read the ledgers by 06:00 and the arrests ran for nine days: twenty-three collectors and two village committees taken on Special Branch warrants, with magistrate review in each case inside 72 hours under the 1964 statute¹¹.

Long An's collections from the posted villages of the three districts fell by about two-thirds through the summer of 1965 and were about a third of the previous year's by December, which cost the Front both money and the rice it bought with it in a province where the titling had already ended rent¹¹. The secretary rebuilt the committee from the Rung Sat by August with cadres sent down from the region, as the Can Giuoc section had been rebuilt before it. What did not come back was the mooring: the committee never again met in a place a boat could reach from a hamlet with a post.

### New: The restricted area over Trung Lap
*7 March 1965 · Trung Lap and Phu Hoa Dong, Hau Nghia Province · EV014-9*

*Initiative: allied*

The provision's first near-disaster was procedural and it is worth one event, because the procedure is most of what the new headquarters was for. On the night of 7 March 1965 an assault team raided a house at Trung Lap on a Hau Nghia file. MACV-JSOC's operations centre declared a restricted operating area of two kilometres' radius for four hours and passed it, as its standing procedure required, to the ARVN 25th Division, the province chief, the sector adviser and the combined command's III Corps centre¹¹. It did not reach the Popular Forces platoon at the post 1,400 metres away, because the sector's night net closed at 22:00 and the platoon had no radio of its own until the Go Vap sets arrived later that year. The platoon heard helicopters and small-arms fire at 01:50 inside its own village, stood to, and its leader took a squad up the hamlet path toward the noise. Delta's team, coming out with a prisoner, identified the squad at about 120 metres through goggles and went flat in a ditch until it passed; nobody fired.

Vance changed the procedure within the week: from 15 March a restricted area was passed down to the platoon holding the ground or it was not declared, which in the first year cancelled eleven raids outright¹¹. The incident is the clearest statement in the record of what the headquarters' deconfliction duty costs and buys. It buys the lives of the men on both ends of a hamlet path. It costs eleven targets in a year, and it is the reason a provision that needs a secret needs a joint headquarters more than it needs another squadron.

## Phase II — The main force war (Aug 1965 – Dec 1967)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1967 the United States has about 486,000 military personnel in Vietnam and has lost 9,378 of them killed by hostile action in the year¹². Rolling Thunder has dropped about 864,000 tons on North Vietnam by the Pentagon's announcement of 31 December¹³, and the North's air defences have made every strike near Hanoi expensive. The Trail is carrying more than ever; truck movements rise sharply from October to December. The enemy order of battle is in dispute: MACV counts about 300,000 communist personnel, the CIA up to 430,000¹⁴, and the disagreement turns on whether the guerrillas and the political infrastructure, the part of the enemy the main-force war does not touch, are counted at all.

On 21 November Westmoreland tells the National Press Club that the enemy is "unable to mount a major offensive" and that "the end begins to come into view"¹⁴. The administration's progress campaign of the autumn rests on the body count, the Hamlet Evaluation System and the claim that the crossover point is near. McNamara, who has lost confidence in the war, has announced his departure for the World Bank, and Johnson's offer at San Antonio on 29 September, to stop the bombing in exchange for prompt and productive talks, has been rejected by Hanoi. In Saigon there is, for the first time since 1963, an elected government under Thieu, and in the countryside CORDS has begun to organize the territorial war, from a less low base than history's. About 820,000 hectares have been titled to about 640,000 families, rent has ended in law and largely in fact wherever the government holds the night, and the Commission has convicted a general. The infrastructure of the Front is smaller in the Delta than on the historical course, and its tax take lower, but it is intact in every hamlet the government does not hold after dark, and those hamlets are still most of the contested countryside¹.

In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.

In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest². The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.

The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North¹⁵. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.

The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.

The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.

Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁴. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.

The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it⁵. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.

The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire⁶. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.

The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁷. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.

The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁸. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.

The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's⁹. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.

Over the North the phase ends with the campaign the theater asked for and the result it predicted. In October 1966 this command reported that the northern campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed and that the North's war in the South needed none of it, and the barrier began from that report. The air defence that history's gradualism let the North build under sanctuary was built instead under fire and from China: about 120 MiGs fighting from Chinese fields, and SA-2 battalions three sites to a launcher. About 40–90 fewer American aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67 than historically, and the Stennis hearings on the restrictions were never held¹⁰.

Delta ends the phase with its rate found and its limit found with it. Thirty-eight raids a month in 1966 and 44 in 1967, 297 listed cadre at district level or above in the two years, 61 of them province or region committee members, and nine finance sections taken with their ledgers; four in five of the raids in III and IV Corps, because that is where the file is. Ninety-four reconnaissance missions into the Laotian panhandle under the ambassador's limits produced the first measured coordinates under canopy in this war and changed what arrives in the South by one to four points, inside the width the phase already holds¹¹. Fourteen operators are dead, four missing near the Ban Laboy ford, fifty-one wounded, and about a quarter of the men in the assault troops were selected after the war began, because the unit was committed whole and has nowhere to rotate to. And in the upper Delta the enemy has answered the whole provision with three sentences in a COSVN circular: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet, committees meet across the border, couriers carry nothing written. The committees of Dinh Tuong now govern their districts from Memot at two months' remove, their collections at about a sixth of 1964's, and the raid yield that measures this success is falling.

> 
> In Hanoi the decision is taken. The PAVN and VC main forces have been drawn to the borders and have drawn the Americans after them; the VC's local forces and cadres in and around the cities are preparing; and the Politburo has set the Tet holiday of 1968 as the moment for the General Offensive and General Uprising. The phase ends with each side certain that the other is weaker than it is, and with the population of the South, the object of the war, still largely outside the reach of either army's strategy.
> 
> In the held belt the resident infrastructure has been driven out of most villages with settled posts by the end of 1967, and the arrest count has fallen because there is little left there to arrest². The National Police numbers about 80,000, the chiefs have mostly held their districts for two or three years, and the Front's legal cadres are in the towns, where the police knows less.
> 
> The enemy's external supply is measured: the Trail by the panhandle watch, Sihanoukville by the count, the North's roads by the Gulf watch, and every measure says that what arrives exceeds what the South's forces need from the North¹⁵. That knowledge is honest from 1965 rather than from 1970, and it has not changed the rules, the bombing or the strategy. Its main effect on Washington has been to deliver bad news early.
> 
> The RVNAF enters 1968 with the rifles it has carried for four years and a Regional Force that the corps commanders want for their own operations, bound since 1967 by the rule that keeps it in its provinces. The American army has had no rifle crisis and no inquiry, and has lost somewhat fewer men in the first minutes of its fights; it is the same army in every other respect, fighting the same battles on the enemy's terms.
> 
> The bombers have learned two things in two years: that a bridge they can measure dies in a night and is replaced by five crossings they cannot, and that a siege they can measure becomes the enemy's worst battle. The second lesson is the one the headquarters remembers going into 1968.
> 
> Phung Hoang has a centre in every district and an audited count of about 18,000 neutralized since 1965, about one in five of them members of district or village committees, and the Front's district administration in the held belt now governs from the contested edge by courier. The word Phoenix has been a press story since March 1967. About 7,000 selected advisers hold every field post below corps; the American battalions have changed over once or twice each as units, have fought better in the contacts they were granted, and have learned at Dien Ban to keep their reliefs off the dark of the moon. The staggered six-week overlap that followed raised the peak American strength in theater by about 15,000–25,000 men, which the expansion battalions of 1967 waited for, so that the enemy's tactic against the relief was paid for in American spaces rather than American dead⁴. None of it has changed who chooses the battle.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with about four in five of its battalions commanded by officers the board chose, on eighteen-month commands, with the captain-led battalion nearly gone and the thirty-day review feared and read; about a third fewer of its battalions have been rendered ineffective in 1966–67 than on the historical course, which no report shows because the enemy declined the fights that would have shown it⁵. The 25th Division has a commander from the list and the corps have the commanders they had. The Military Security Service has its first file on the board's officers as a political factor, and COSVN has had every list the board published.
> 
> The factories end 1967 producing what the domestic share buys, with the steelworks short of power and the arsenal short of its gunners' trust after Phu Cat. Every post of the held belt has a radio, the Front attacks those that can call about a third less often than those that cannot, and where the guns can reach the posts the first call is for fire⁶. The posts hold themselves better than the hamlets around them.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 trained to the man; training alone would have left it as short of squad leaders as history's, and what filled most of the empty slots was the NCO schooling described below; its battalions have lost about a tenth to a sixth fewer men in the ambushes the enemy still lays, beyond what the rifles and the officers saved, and about one in eight fewer battalions has been broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms alone would have left. The drill-sergeant corps has begun to return about 650–1,800 platoon sergeants a year to the battalions⁷. In the lowlands of Quang Nam and Quang Ngai the mine has replaced the firefight as the enemy's way of killing Americans, and in the districts around Saigon the Front's guerrilla squads are drilled by men the Republic trained.
> 
> The ARVN ends 1967 with its squads and platoons led by schooled men: about two in three of the slots the field commissions emptied are held by corporals first class who passed the leader's course, and the squads of the 7th Division held their base of fire at Hau My when their officers fell. I judge that about one in six to one in five fewer ARVN battalions were broken in 1966–67 than the officer reforms and the basic course alone would have left, and that the posts of the Delta lost about a tenth to a fifth fewer to night attack than the radio and the trained platoon had already saved⁸. None of it shows in a return: the enemy attacked less what kept its routine. American sergeants pass the Basic Leader Course at Bien Hoa or wait for it, and the waiver of 1966 has become a ninety-day deferral.
> 
> The combined command ends 1967 with one corps area under a Vietnamese commander and three under American deputies who in practice run them, a quarterly plan the corps commanders execute at their own speed, and a two-layer plan that protects its operations and insults its Vietnamese staff. The task force has broken the Front's district government of the Saigon belt from its edge: the Hoc Mon committee and the region's finance section govern from the Ho Bo woods, and the region's collections from the posted villages are about an eighth of 1964's⁹. On the II Corps coast it has a list it abandoned and a story the Front still tells.
> 
> Over the North the phase ends with the campaign the theater asked for and the result it predicted. In October 1966 this command reported that the northern campaign was destroying everything in the North that could be destroyed and that the North's war in the South needed none of it, and the barrier began from that report. The air defence that history's gradualism let the North build under sanctuary was built instead under fire and from China: about 120 MiGs fighting from Chinese fields, and SA-2 battalions three sites to a launcher. About 40–90 fewer American aircraft were lost over the North in 1966–67 than historically, and the Stennis hearings on the restrictions were never held¹⁰.

### New: The rhythm of the raid, 1965–1967
*1 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The Saigon belt (Gia Dinh, Long An, Hau Nghia, Bien Hoa), the upper Delta (Dinh Tuong, Kien Hoa, Vinh Long, Phong Dinh) and the coastal lowlands of Binh Dinh and Quang Ngai · EV014-3*

*Initiative: allied*

By the spring of 1966 the unit had found its rate, and the rate was not the one the first months had promised. Three assault squadrons forward gave six assault troops, and six troops with six to twenty-four hours of planning behind each raid produced 38 raids a month on average in 1966 and 44 in 1967 — with one month, March 1966, at 104 after the Dinh Tuong finance section's courier book fell into the task force's hands, and April at 19 while the squadrons that had flown it stood down¹¹. Reconnaissance ran at nine to twelve teams in the field at once, each out three to six days, and the two could not be run at full stretch together: a squadron raiding in Kien Hoa was not watching a trail junction in the Do Xa.

The yield was concentrated and it was real. Of about 1,000 raids in the thirty months, 171 reached a listed cadre at district level or above in 1966 and 126 in 1967, with 61 province or region committee members among them over the two years and nine finance sections taken with their ledgers¹¹. Four in five of those raids were in III and IV Corps, where the files were thick, and the squadron at Da Nang spent most of 1966 and 1967 on reconnaissance rather than raiding because the coastal hamlets of Quang Ngai had no file worth raiding on and the Front held them at night. In the Highlands the unit worked only as reconnaissance in the tri-border, where it had no file, no language and no Montagnard source it could use without an interpreter the enemy might own.

The price was paid in the one currency the unit could not print. Between August 1965 and December 1967 Delta lost fourteen operators killed, four missing in Laos and fifty-one wounded, with two of E Squadron's helicopters shot down over the Rung Sat and the Plain of Reeds¹¹. Fort Bragg returned thirty to fifty operators a year from a selection course run by a cadre that was itself in Vietnam, so the unit held its numbers and spent its experience: by the end of 1967 about a quarter of the men in the assault troops had been selected and trained after the war began.

### New: The road watch: Delta in Laos
*20 Oct 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The Laotian panhandle: Routes 9, 92 and 912, the Ban Laboy ford, the Mu Gia and Ban Karai passes · EV014-4*

*Initiative: allied*

Washington authorised cross-border reconnaissance in Laos on 21 September 1965 and SOG's first team went 24 km in against target D-1 on 18 October¹⁶¹⁷. Delta's teams went in behind SOG's on the same authority and under the same limits: Ambassador Sullivan in Vientiane set the depth, the targets and the length of each mission, and no exploitation force followed. Two to four Delta teams of five were in the panhandle at a time from 20 October 1965, watching the stretches the Global Hawk's radar could see from above and not under the trees.

What the teams added was accuracy and survival. A SOG team of two or three Americans and three to twelve indigenous soldiers moved by day, navigated by map and called a FAC overhead to relay; a Delta team moved at night on goggles and spoke to Tan Son Nhut by satellite with its position to a few metres (E01). Of 94 Delta missions into the panhandle in 1966–67, 71 were completed without the team being compromised, against a SOG rate nearer one in three¹¹¹⁶. The product went into STEADY COUNT's track list and the coordinate cell's folders: 84 truck parks, 31 gun positions and 19 storage points measured to a few metres, about a third of them under canopy where no other instrument in this war could find anything at all.

It changed what arrived in the South by almost nothing. Group 559 had answered HARD CROSSING in 1966 by owning nothing that could be measured, and a braided net of fords and night pontoons does not care how exactly one of its crossings is known. The teams' cueing taxed the flow by perhaps one to four points more than the radar alone, inside the width the phase already holds. It cost nine Americans killed or missing in two years, including Captain Robert L. Ainsley's team of five, lost whole near the Ban Laboy ford between 11 and 14 July 1967 after two days of transmissions and then nothing, to a 559th Group security battalion that had learned by then to hunt the watchers¹¹.

### New: The empty beds of Dinh Tuong
*4 Sep – 14 Nov 1967 · Cai Lay, Cai Be and Giao Duc Districts, Dinh Tuong Province; Memot, Kampong Cham Province, Cambodia · EV014-5*

*Initiative: both*

This is the operation that taught the command what the unit had actually done, and it did so by failing for ten weeks.

In the first week of September 1967 the National Fusion Centre gave the Can Tho squadron twenty-six addresses in the three upper districts of Dinh Tuong: the province committee's five surviving members, the finance section's chief, and twenty of the collectors and couriers who had been named in the ledgers taken in 1966. The file was the best in the Delta. The province had a post in every village the government held, a resident constable in most of them, a family census three years deep and a land register that said who tilled what. Between 4 September and 14 November the squadron mounted twenty-three raids on those addresses, most of them inside two hours of the decision and all at night.

It took two. A courier of nineteen was lifted out of a house in Cai Be on 19 September with a bag of receipts, and a village committee secretary at Giao Duc on 2 October. The other twenty-one raids found a bed that had been slept in and a family that said, truthfully, that the man had not been there for months.

The courier told them why, and the task force's interrogators had it out of her in two days. The province committee had not lived in Dinh Tuong since March. It lived at Memot, in the rubber across the Cambodian border, with the region's finance section, and it came into the province for four or five nights every second month, moving every night, sleeping in a different hamlet each time and never in a house named in a ledger. The rule had come down in a COSVN circular in April 1967, over Pham Hung's name — he had taken the Central Office when Nguyen Chi Thanh died in Hanoi in July, and the circular was Thanh's last instruction carried out by his successor¹⁸. It had three sentences in it: senior cadre do not sleep twice in a hamlet; committees meet in the base areas or across the border and never in villages; couriers carry nothing written.

At Tan Son Nhut in November the argument ran the way arguments about metrics run. The unit's raid yield in the Delta had fallen by about two-fifths from 1966 and the natural reading was that the squadron had gone slack. Vance's J-2 and the task force's analysts read it the other way and were right: the committees of the upper Delta had been driven out of the province they administered, were running it by courier from across an international border at two months' remove, and the falling yield was the measure of that success and not of failure. The Front paid for it in the only currency it had to pay in. The province's collections from the posted villages ran at about a sixth of 1964's through 1967, its rice procurement in the three districts fell with them, and the committee that had once set a village's tax rate in person now learned of a bad harvest six weeks after it happened¹¹. It did not pay in people. The adaptation cost the Front a courier's walking time, which against 1,310 Americans and the best three hundred operators in their army is the cheapest answer any provision in this record has drawn from the enemy.

The command changed its measure in December 1967. Delta's reporting after that gave the raid count, and beside it the Front's collections in the raided districts and the distance the committees lived from them.

## Phase III — Tet and its aftermath (Jan 1968 – Dec 1968)

### New: Delta at Tet: the command posts in Saigon and the files at Hue
*29 Jan – 8 Mar 1968 · Saigon (Districts 5, 6 and 8, the Phu Tho racetrack, Gia Dinh); Hue · EV014-6*

*Initiative: enemy*

In the ten days before Tet the unit raided eleven addresses in Gia Dinh and Saigon out of the task force's file and took two couriers of the city's sapper organisation, on 24 and 27 January. Neither knew anything about the timing of the offensive, and neither did the file. The national file named the Front's political apparatus, street by street in places, and the apparatus is not where the decision to attack at Tet was held or when it was transmitted; that is the finding the record had already made and this memorandum confirms from the other side of the same week¹¹. The warning that reached the corps came from the task force's and MACV's reading of the troop movements, not from Delta's prisoners.

Once the attack came, the unit was used for what it was best at and not for what it was built for. Between 1 and 9 February three assault troops cleared fourteen Front command posts in Districts 5, 6 and 8 and around the Phu Tho racetrack, moving at night with goggles against men who had never fought anyone who could see in the dark; eight of the fourteen were taken without a shot fired at the entry. It was the best urban assault force in the theater and it was spent as infantry for nine days. It cost nine operators killed and thirty-one wounded, the unit's worst month of the war, about a tenth of the operators then in the country¹¹.

At Hue a troop was flown in on 9 February on Vance's own authority with two Special Branch officers, to the Special Branch compound inside the triangle, to recover the province's and districts' infrastructure files before the Front's security service could finish with them. It recovered two of the seven district files and the province register's index. The rest had gone north with the Front's security cadres in the first week, as the record has it¹¹. Two operators were killed in the compound's courtyard on 10 February. The judgment the memorandum takes from that morning is narrow and worth stating: a raid force can recover files a few days late and cannot prevent their capture, and the record's own account of what Hue cost the file-building effort stands unaltered.

### New: The 81st Special Group: a Vietnamese unit beside Delta
*1 Mar 1968 – 31 Dec 1971 · Long Thanh, Bien Hoa Province; the Special Warfare Centre at Nha Trang; Tan Son Nhut · EV014-8*

*Initiative: allied*

MACV-JSOC proposed a Vietnamese counterpart unit in October 1967 and the Joint General Staff agreed in February 1968, with Tet's lesson fresh: the best urban night force in the country was American and would go home. Selection opened at Long Thanh on 1 March 1968 from the Rangers, the airborne division and the Luc Luong Dac Biet, run by Delta's training element on its own four-week course; 23 of 214 candidates passed the first board and 14 finished the six-month operator course¹¹. The first squadron of the 81st Special Group, about 70 operators under Major Nguyen Van Thuan, was operational in November 1969; a second followed in May 1971.

It was given the war's instruments as they existed in 1969 and not Delta's. AN/PVS-2 starlight scopes rather than fused goggles, AN/PRC-25s rather than satellite radios, and lift from the VNAF's 219th Helicopter Squadron rather than from E Squadron¹¹. On a clear night it worked at perhaps half Delta's standard and on a wet one at a quarter, and its raids in Kien Hoa and Dinh Tuong in 1970–71 took district cadre rather than province committees, because the targets its American partner reached were across a border it was not sent over.

Two things about it belong in the record. The first is where it lived: the palace watched it from the day it was proposed, the Joint General Staff's special warfare directorate held it under a standing order that no element of it would be stationed within Saigon, and its families were housed inside the Long Thanh compound on rations drawn against the garrison's — which is why its desertion ran at about a fifth of the ARVN's rate in 1971, when a soldier's pay bought a third less rice than in 1966¹¹. A unit that can take a guarded house at night is a unit that can take a palace, and every general in Saigon had done that arithmetic before the first course ended. The second is what it inherited when Delta left: its training, its selection standard and nothing else that mattered. The goggles, the satellite radios, the helicopters and the folders went home with the Americans in 1973.

### New: The ambush at Thanh Phu
*18 June 1968 · Thanh Phu District, Kien Hoa Province · EV014-10*

*Initiative: enemy*

The unit's worst single hour in the Delta was the consequence the dossier had named and the record had been waiting for. In June 1968, with the Front's Kien Hoa committee reconstituting after its Tet losses, the Can Tho squadron raided on a file that had come to the task force through a Vietnamese province intelligence section rather than through the Special Branch. The target was a committee finance cadre in a house on a canal at Thanh Phu, named by a source the section would not identify.

The house was occupied by a reinforced guerrilla platoon with two RPD machine guns sited on the only dry approach, and the team walked into it at 02:20 on 18 June. Two operators were killed in the first fifteen seconds and three wounded, one of them the team leader; the team broke contact into the canal, called the squadron's reaction team and two VNAF gunships of the 217th Squadron, and was out by 04:10¹¹. The enemy left eleven dead when the gunships came.

The section's source was never produced. The task force's counter-intelligence staff concluded in August that the enemy had either planted the target or learned of it inside the province section, and could not say which, which is the condition the record has described since 1964 (INTEL.penetration, POS002-3)¹¹. The effect on practice was immediate and permanent: from September 1968 MACV-JSOC would not raid on a single-source target that had not passed through the Special Branch or the National Fusion Centre, which closed a channel the unit had used perhaps a dozen times a year. The judgment belongs in the record at its real weight. A raid force that cannot read the language it operates in is only as safe as the files it is handed, and this is the mechanism the dossier named before it happened (F014-22, D6 of P014a).

## Phase IV — Vietnamization and drawdown (Jan 1969 – Dec 1971)

### New: The Cambodian folders
*1 Jan 1969 – 30 Jun 1970 · Base Areas 350, 351, 352, 353, 609 and 740, the Fishhook and the Parrot's Beak; Memot and Snoul, Kampong Cham Province; Kratie · EV014-7*

*Initiative: allied*

American teams could enter Cambodia from September 1967, on foot, without tactical air, without a forward air controller overhead and with no exploitation force behind them, and those limits held until the incursion. Delta put teams across on those terms from 12 September 1967 and ran 61 missions into the base areas in 1969 beside SOG's 454¹⁶. The teams walked in from the border at night, lay up under the rubber by day, and counted: ninety-four cache sites, thirty-one of them under permanent roofing, eleven field hospitals, four vehicle parks and the Memot headquarters complex's outer security, which was three concentric belts of bunkers manned by a battalion¹¹. The Global Hawk's radar had been counting the road traffic from Sihanoukville to those same base areas since 1965 and could not see a cache under rubber. The folders the teams built are what the incursion's forces worked from on 29 April 1970, and they are part of why the caches fell in days rather than weeks.

COSVN was never in them. The Central Office was about 2,400 people who moved between bunkers and meeting houses by bicycle, warned of B-52 raids from 1968 by Soviet trawlers reporting the bombers' course, and it went northwest to Kratie on 19 March 1970, six weeks before the incursion crossed the border¹⁸. Delta's teams watched the Memot complex for eleven nights in February 1970 and reported what the complex was: a rear-service and signals installation whose senior occupants had left. The provision names COSVN as a mission; the constraint set declined it from the first day and the enemy's own mobility declined it again.

### No longer happens: The Son Tay raid
*21 Nov 1970 · Son Tay prison camp, about 37 km west of Hanoi · EV000-69*

*Initiative: neither*

The raid of 21 November 1970 was not flown in this war, and the reason is the reconnaissance that the historical operation did not have.

Planning began on 9 May 1970 and the joint task force under Brigadier General LeRoy J. Manor and Colonel Arthur D. Simons trained through the summer at Eglin, as historically¹⁹. On 14 October, with the operation six weeks out, MACV-JSOC proposed what no American force had been able to offer in 1970 and this one could: two men of G Squadron on the ground. They went in on the night of 21 October by an HH-3E flying a Trail infiltration profile, lay on the wooded slope 1,400 metres southeast of the camp for three nights with a thermal sight and a satellite radio, and reported on 24 October that the compound held a guard element of perhaps forty men, that the cells were unoccupied, that no cooking was done for prisoners and that no prisoner was taken to the wells, which were dry and partly collapsed¹¹. The prisoners had been moved on 14 July 1970 to the camp the prisoners themselves called Camp Faith, about 24 km closer to Hanoi²⁰. The Joint Chiefs cancelled the operation on 2 November 1970.

What the cancellation saved is easy to count: 116 aircraft committed, 56 Special Forces soldiers landed 37 km from Hanoi, an HH-3E deliberately crashed inside the compound, an F-105G lost to an SA-2, two raiders wounded and about 42 PAVN guards killed²⁰. What it cost is the part worth recording, because it was a cost nobody weighed at the time. Historically the raid failed in its purpose and succeeded in another: Hanoi read it as proof that its camps in the countryside could be reached, consolidated its prisoners into the central prisons in Hanoi over the following months, and many of the prisoners who came home in 1973 said their treatment and their morale improved from that winter¹⁹. In this war the raid is not flown, the consolidation does not happen, and the American prisoners stay dispersed in the camps outside Hanoi through 1971 and 1972 under the regime they had before — and they never learn that anyone came for them. A better reconnaissance capability cancelled an operation whose military result was nil and whose moral result was not.

**Before:**

> On the night of 20–21 November 1970 a joint task force under Brigadier General LeRoy J. Manor and Colonel Arthur D. Simons landed 56 Special Forces soldiers by HH-53 and HH-3E helicopters, guided by C-130 Combat Talons, at the prison camp at Son Tay to rescue about 61 American prisoners. Navy aircraft from USS *Oriskany* and USS *Ranger* flew a diversion over Haiphong, and F-105G Wild Weasels suppressed the SA-2 sites. The camp was empty: the prisoners had been moved in July, which intelligence learned only days before. The raiders lost two wounded, an HH-3E deliberately crash-landed inside the compound and an F-105G to a SAM; they reported 42 guards killed, a Vietnamese source six guards and seven civilians. The raid failed in its purpose but succeeded in another: Hanoi consolidated its prisoners in central prisons in Hanoi, and many returning prisoners said their treatment and morale improved¹⁹.

### New: Cooper–Church takes the teams out
*29 Dec 1970 – 31 Dec 1971 · The Laotian panhandle; the Cambodian base areas; Tan Son Nhut · EV014-11*

*Initiative: neither*

The provision's cross-border work ended by Act of Congress, five years and three months after it began, and it ended for reasons that had nothing to do with it. The Cooper–Church amendment of 29 December 1970 barred American ground troops and advisers from Laos and Cambodia. MACV's lawyers read it as covering reconnaissance teams, CINCPAC agreed in January 1971, and Vance pulled the last two Delta teams out of the Laotian panhandle on 19 January and cancelled the February programme into Base Areas 353 and 609¹¹.

The timing could hardly have been worse for the thing the teams were best at. Lam Son 719 crossed into Laos on 8 February 1971 with ARVN divisions and no American ground element of any kind, against the terrain and the 559th Group's security forces that Delta's teams had been watching since 1965. The folders existed; the men who made them could not go. What the ARVN had instead was imagery, the panhandle radar watch and a Vietnamese reconnaissance effort of its own. Through the rest of 1971 the squadrons raided inside the South at about 30 a month, took district cadre, and ran reconnaissance in the base areas of the South; the 81st Special Group's second squadron stood up at Long Thanh in May.

The event is in the record because of what it says about the provision's whole class. The cross-border reconnaissance was the one thing Delta did that nothing else in this war could do, it was never authorised by anything more durable than an ambassador's discretion, and it was taken away in a sentence of a defence appropriations bill written about a different problem.
